tagline.text: Manila's former Plaza Lawton, with the Bonifacio statue in front of the post office

location.label: Location
location.text: Eastern end of Padre Burgos Avenue, Ermita, Manila, in front of the Manila Central Post Office

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–300 (free entry; snacks and transport included, based on 1 hour)

children.text: Liwasang Bonifacio is a plaza in Ermita, Manila, in front of the Manila Central Post Office. At its center stands a bronze statue of Andrés Bonifacio, who founded the Katipunan, the Philippine independence movement. Formerly called Plaza Lawton, it was declared a National Historical Landmark in 2012.

Liwasang Bonifacio is a city plaza that straddles the boundary between Ermita and Intramuros in Manila. "Liwasan" means plaza in Tagalog, so the name can be rendered as "Bonifacio Square." From the south bank of the Pasig River, Jones Bridge, MacArthur Bridge and Quezon Bridge all lead to this plaza, and at its southern end Padre Burgos Avenue runs toward Rizal Park. That makes the plaza a gateway for anyone crossing the river from Quiapo, Santa Cruz or Binondo into Ermita and Intramuros. To the north stands the neoclassical Manila Central Post Office, and on one side is the Manila Metropolitan Theater, a 1930s building, so you can see some of Old Manila's best-known buildings in one stop.

The history of this spot goes back to the Spanish era. The present plaza and post office stand on the site of the Cuartel del Fortín, a small fortress that guarded the Pasig River, and the plaza in front of it was called Plaza del Fortín. With its stone benches and trees, it is said to have been a place where residents gathered in the evenings to enjoy musical performances. In the late 19th century a large tobacco factory called the Fábrica del Fortín was built on the fortress grounds and is said to have employed more than 5,000 workers, and in the American period the Bureau of Posts and later the present Central Post Office took its place. The area was also originally the site of the Parián de Arroceros, a Chinese market quarter.

In the early 20th century, during the American period, the plaza was renamed Plaza Lawton. The name honored U.S. Major General Henry Ware Lawton, who was killed by a sniper at the Battle of San Mateo during the Philippine–American War and is known as the highest-ranking American officer to die in that war. A Manila tranvía (tram) terminal stood here, and later the plaza became a transfer point for jeepneys and buses. Manileños still call this area "Lawton," and they know the neighborhood around LRT-1 Central Terminal station and the bus terminal by that name. When asking for directions, it helps to know that "Liwasang Bonifacio" and "Lawton" are the same place.

The plaza took its present name in 1963. For the centennial of the birth of Andrés Bonifacio, founder of the Katipunan, it was renamed Liwasang Bonifacio, and a bronze statue of Bonifacio by National Artist Guillermo Tolentino was set up at its center. During the martial law years and afterward, the plaza was a stage for rallies and protests, and the City of Manila lists it as one of its "freedom parks," where people may assemble without a permit. In 2012 the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) declared the plaza a National Historical Landmark to protect it from urban development. As a travel destination, the plaza is not a place of dazzling sights. The Bonifacio statue, the fountain, the palms and the post office across the road are all there is, so it is not somewhere to linger long. Its value lies instead as a starting point or stopover on a walk through Old Manila. It sits at the center of routes to Intramuros, Rizal Park, the National Museum, and across the Pasig River to Quiapo and Binondo, which makes it handy for planning your day. This guide covers what to see at the plaza, a walking order, how to get there, costs and cautions. Conditions on the ground change often, so check the latest news before you go.

blocks.title: The Andrés Bonifacio statue by Tolentino

children.text: The bronze statue at the center of the plaza is the work of National Artist Guillermo Tolentino and was erected in 1963 to mark the centennial of Bonifacio's birth. It is described as showing a calm, dignified stance with the hands near the bolo (knife). An NHCP historical marker stands on the pedestal, so read the explanatory text in Filipino as well. Unlike the Rizal Monument in Rizal Park, it has no fence or honor guard, so you can see it up close.

The Manila Central Post Office across from the plaza is a neoclassical building designed by architects Juan Arellano and Tomás Mapúa and completed in 1928. Its location was well placed for mail arriving by way of the Pasig River, and it long served as the center of postal operations. After it was heavily damaged by a fire in 2023, restoration plans were announced, so check on the spot whether you can see the exterior or enter the building.

In the 2002 renovation, with help from the Heritage Conservation Society, a fountain was placed in the middle of the plaza and tall royal palms were lined up on both sides, framing the front of the post office. The area around the fountain is a good place for a short rest in downtown Manila, and cyclists touring Old Manila also use it as a rest stop.

blocks.title: The Pasig riverfront where three bridges meet

children.text: The plaza is where the southern ends of Jones Bridge, MacArthur Bridge and Quezon Bridge come together. Crossing the bridges takes you to Binondo, Santa Cruz and Quiapo, so it is a fork in the road for a tour of Old Manila. Walking along the river, you get a real sense that Manila grew up along the Pasig.

blocks.title: From Plaza Lawton to Bonifacio: a history of names

children.text: This plaza has had three names: Plaza del Fortín in the Spanish era, Plaza Lawton in the American era, and Liwasang Bonifacio since 1963. The political currents from the colonial period to independence are reflected in its names. Guidebooks and maps mix "Lawton" and "Bonifacio," so remember that they are the same place.

blocks.title: A freedom park, the plaza of protests and rallies

children.text: During the martial law years and afterward, this plaza was a protest site for youth and labor groups. The City of Manila describes it as a freedom park where rallies can be held without a permit, and in July 2026 a large rally by a religious group was held at the plaza, after which the city suspended school classes, according to news reports. On days when a rally is held, traffic in the surrounding area may be restricted, so it is best to check the news before you visit.

blocks.title: The streetscape linking Old Manila's buildings

children.text: On one side of the plaza is the Manila Metropolitan Theater, close by is Manila City Hall, and not far off is Mehan Garden. All of them form part of a string of works by architect Juan Arellano in Old Manila, and since they are within walking distance, they make a good short architecture walk to continue on.

items.title: A 30-minute to 1-hour plaza visit
items.subtitle: Statue, fountain and post office building

children.text: Arrive by LRT-1 Central Terminal station or by taxi and start at the southern end of the plaza. In the morning the light is soft and photos come out well.
In front of the Bonifacio statue, look at the NHCP marker on the pedestal and at the sculpture. Photograph the front of the post office together with the fountain and royal palms in the background.
Cross the road to see the exterior of the Manila Central Post Office, then walk toward the Manila Metropolitan Theater. Access may be restricted because of restoration work.
Go to the riverside to look at Jones Bridge and Quezon Bridge, then move on to your next destination.
Traffic around the plaza is very complicated. Cross only at signals and crossings.

items.title: Half-day Old Manila route
items.subtitle: Lawton, the Metropolitan Theater and Intramuros

children.text: See the statue and the exterior of the post office at Liwasang Bonifacio.
Look at the exterior of the Manila Metropolitan Theater, and check on the spot whether performances or tours are running.
Walk along Padre Burgos Avenue to
Intramuros
. Visit Manila Cathedral and San Agustin Church in turn.
Have lunch at a restaurant inside Intramuros. Check opening hours locally.
Take a taxi or Grab to
Rizal Park
or back to your hotel. Adjust the schedule to the weather.

From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) or your hotel in Manila, take a taxi or Grab and set "Liwasang Bonifacio" or "Lawton" as the destination. "Lawton" is the more familiar name to Manileños.
Travel time and fares vary greatly with traffic, so check locally.
During rush hour the Old Manila area is very congested.

LRT-1 Central Terminal station (formerly Arroceros station) is close to the plaza, on the Antonio Villegas Street side near Manila City Hall and the Central Post Office. It is the last LRT-1 station south of the Pasig River.

Next to the station are the Lawton Park N' Ride bus terminal and, it is said, the Lawton landing (on Muelle del Rio Street) for the Pasig River ferry. As of 2026 guides, departures run roughly 8 am to 5 pm and the service is listed as free, but it sometimes stops for maintenance and its days and operation change, so check with the MMDA or locally.

Intramuros, Manila City Hall and the Metropolitan Theater are all within walking distance. It is hot at midday, so bring shade and water, and at night a taxi or Grab is safer even for short distances.

Liwasang Bonifacio is an open-air plaza, so the dry season, when there is little rain and it is cooler, is the best time to go. At midday, when the sun is high, there is little shade and it is hot. In the morning or late afternoon the light is soft and good for photographing the statue.
On days with protests or rallies, traffic is heavy and the plaza gets crowded. Around Bonifacio Day on November 30 there may be commemorations or rallies, so check the schedule.

There are no hotels or restaurants at Liwasang Bonifacio itself. Most visitors stay in Ermita or Malate, or inside Intramuros, and walk to the plaza. Choose a hotel close to a main road for safety and easy transport.

For meals, use the restaurants in Intramuros or Ermita, or the food courts of nearby shopping malls. Check the hygiene of street food before eating it, and it is safer to drink bottled water. Opening hours and prices at businesses change, so check locally.
"Lawton" and "Liwasang Bonifacio" are the same place, so telling a taxi driver "Lawton" works.
Visit in the morning or late afternoon, when the soft light makes the best photos of the statue.
There is little shade at the plaza, so bring water, a hat and sunscreen.
Combine it with Intramuros, the Metropolitan Theater and the Pasig River bridges for an efficient half-day route.
Keep your phone and camera firmly in hand and keep your wallet in a front pocket to guard against pickpockets.
On days with rallies or protests, expect traffic closures and crowds, so check the news.
Because of the Central Post Office restoration, some areas may be screened off or closed to entry. Check the latest announcements.
Liwasang Bonifacio is a freedom park where protests and rallies are often held. On rally days traffic around it is restricted and crowded, so check the latest news before you go.
The intersection has heavy car and jeepney traffic, so cross only at signals and crossings.
Beware of pickpockets and snatch thieves, and do not show off valuables.
Visitors have reported street vendors, people begging and litter at the plaza. Upkeep may vary from day to day.
Do not linger after dark, and at night travel by taxi or Grab.
Whether the post office restoration and plaza facilities are open can change, so follow the signs on site.
A 1930s Art Deco theater right beside the plaza, the work of architect Juan Arellano. Check locally for interior access and performance schedules.
The Spanish-era walled city within walking distance along Padre Burgos Avenue. It has Manila Cathedral and San Agustin Church.
A city park that continues south from the plaza along Padre Burgos Avenue and holds the Rizal Monument. It is easy to reach by taxi.
A fortress on the Pasig riverbank at the northern end of Intramuros, close to the plaza. Check opening hours locally.
One of the oldest Chinatowns in the world, reached by crossing Jones Bridge. Great for a food crawl.
